title: Use Strategies and Properties to Multiply by 1-Digit Numbers
arc: The palm grove — shade tiles arrive in bundles, the foreman makes a quick promise, the rows hide the total, the roof splits, the courtyard sits awkward, the delivery is delayed, and three methods meet at the gate, until the grove model stands before the council.
sources: CCSS 4.NBT.B.5 (thecorestandards.org): 'Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.'

Data Nuggets (MSU KBS L-TER, NSF DRK-12 funded; datanuggets.org; ERIC EJ1048999): free K-16 activities on authentic research data; students follow the process of science — prediction, visualizing, interpreting, evidence-based claims — and totals across equal trials are multiplication of groups

BetterLesson 4th-grade task 'Multiplication: Arrays and an Expanded Algorithm' (teaching.betterlesson.com lesson 519571): a real per-event × events multiplication task (16 games × 21 and 37 bottles) solved with arrays, the expanded algorithm, and area models

Math Curious, 'Starting with multiplication — arrays and area models activities' (mathcurious.com): array hunts, building arrays with Lego bricks, and exploring the properties of multiplication through building — repeated addition, commutative, associative
Playground Architect PBL (Magicore Learning): grade-4 STEM project-based learning aligned to 4.NBT.B.4/B.5 — model making and cost totals, unit price × quantity with multi-digit multiplication
NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data), grades 3–5: quantitative data collected across multiple trials — totals computed as equal groups (trials × count per trial)

Seed-counting classroom experiments (Little Bins for Little Hands seed-dispersal extension 'How many seeds?'; Providence Children's Museum 'Let's Study Seeds'): real counting experiments that produce equal-group 'how many in all' data — seeds per fruit × fruits

prep.title: The grove briefing was already at home
prep.lead: Before class, the class met the multiplication briefing — the bundle math and three home questions, at each student's own pace.
prep.goal: Recover the first exposure, so the grove work begins with thinking — not with content delivery.
prep.pull: Now the probe: what does the class already hold about multiplying?

diagnose.title: The gap map for the grove site
diagnose.lead: Four checkpoints from the briefing. The class votes what it already holds — we are mapping gaps, not scoring students.
diagnose.goal: Build a gap map: what is known, and what is missing, before the bundles are counted.
diagnose.pull: Knowledge building closes exactly what the map flags.

practice.title: Practice — feedback in seconds, not days
practice.lead: First with the model open, then alone, then the harder lane — every answer met in the moment.
practice.goal: Guided, then independent — with feedback that arrives in seconds, not days.
practice.pull: Now a genuinely new situation from the grove.

critic.title: A genuinely new situation from the grove
critic.lead: The class produces its own work in a situation it has not seen before, then defends it. AI enters here — as a critic, never as an author.
critic.goal: Build the STEM production, transfer the method into new territory, and defend it through critique.
critic.pull: One individual task now decides each student's next path.

home: Five shade tiles, forty to a bundle. What is the total — and which basic fact is carrying it?
Why does 6 × 700 give the same shape as 6 × 7? Which seat does the answer land in, and why?
Write a bundle problem of your own: a basic fact with a bundle of hundreds. What is the total, and where does the zero sit?

claims: I can name a basic fact like 6 × 7 and read off its bundle version, 6 × 700.
I can say which seat a product lands in — not just add a zero.
I can move a basic fact one place to the left for each bundle of ten.
I can check a bundle product by estimating its size first.

independent.prompt: The truck now carries bundles of 300. Six bundles — what is the inventory total?
independent.yes: Yes — 6 × 3 is 18, and the bundle of hundreds moves the 18 into the hundreds: 1,800.
independent.notYet: Not yet — find the basic fact first, then see which seat the bundle moves it into.

harder.prompt: A delivery note reads 7 × 400. Write it as a basic fact with bundles, then check the total two different ways.
harder.answer: 7 × 400 is 7 × 4 = 28, moved into the hundreds: 2,800. Check one: four 400s make 1,600, three more 400s make 1,200, and 1,600 + 1,200 lands on 2,800. Check two: 400 × 10 would be 4,000, and taking away three 400s (1,200) leaves 2,800.

options.task: A bundle-scale model of the tile delivery: build a paper model of the truck and one bundle of 100 tiles, then label the whole delivery as basic fact × bundle, with the seat the answer lands in marked on the model.
options.stem: ask what the delivery totals → plan the scale → build the bundle model → test it against the basic fact × bundle → share it at the dry channel

options.task: A zeros-that-mean poster: take one bundle product from the delivery, show seat by seat where the answer lands and why the zero sits there — no bare zero rule allowed anywhere on the poster.
options.stem: ask why the zero sits where it does → plan the poster → build the seat-by-seat story → test it on a classmate → share it on the wall

options.task: A 60-second basic-fact-to-bundle clip: ask the AI to propose five bundle products, judge each on camera by its basic fact, and catch any one it gets wrong. The AI proposes, you decide — the verdicts are the work.
options.stem: ask what a bundle product hides → plan the clip → request five bundle products from the AI (check each with the basic fact) → test your verdicts on camera → share it on the wall

wall.artifact: The bundle inventory — the class's scale model, zero-meaning poster, and bundle verdicts

home: 6 × 512 — round the 512 to a friendly hundred, then estimate the product. What promise could you make with that number?
Why round one factor and not both? What happens to the basic fact if you round both?
The foreman promises four loads of about 300 tiles each. Is that about 1,200 tiles? What would you check first?

claims: I can round a many-digit factor to a friendly hundred before multiplying.
I can keep the one-digit factor exact so the basic fact survives the estimate.
I can judge a promise as reasonable or unreasonable from the estimate alone.
I can say which side of the exact product my estimate sits on.

independent.prompt: The foreman promises the side yard gets 7 rows of 264 tiles. Estimate the product by rounding the 264 — what do you tell him?
independent.yes: Yes — 264 sits past halfway to 300, so round it to 300 and keep the 7: 7 × 300 = 2,100. The promise stands, a little on the safe side.
independent.notYet: Not yet — round the many-digit factor to a friendly hundred, keep the one-digit factor exact, and multiply the friendly pair.

harder.prompt: The foreman's real count is 7 × 264. Find the exact product, then say how close his estimate of 2,100 came.
harder.answer: 7 × 264 = 1,848, so the 2,100 estimate ran 252 high — close enough to keep the promise, not close enough to bill the grove. The estimate sat above the exact product because 264 was rounded up.

options.task: A 60-second promise-defense presentation: take one of the foreman's promises from the morning, show the estimate that backs it, and state how far the estimate could be from the exact product.
options.stem: ask which promise to defend → plan the estimate → build the friendly pair → test it against the exact product → share it at the dry channel

options.task: A promise map: mark the day's promises on a line from estimate to exact product, and label each one keep or break — with the estimate that decided it written under the point.
options.stem: ask which promises to test → plan the line → plot the estimate and the exact for each → test every label against the numbers → share it at the gate

options.task: An AI-stress-tested promise poster: ask the AI to propose three new foreman promises (rows × tiles), verify every one with your own estimate, and show on the poster where the AI's arithmetic slipped — if it slipped at all.
options.stem: ask what makes a promise testable → plan the poster → request three promises from the AI (verify every product yourself) → test each with an estimate → share it on the wall

home: 3 rows of 26 chairs. Split the 26 into 20 + 6 and multiply both parts by 3 — what are the two partial products, and the total?
Why is 3 × 26 the same total as 26 rows of 3? Which way does the grove read its arrays, and does it matter?
Draw an array of 4 rows of 15. Split the row length two different ways and write the partial products for each split.

claims: I can read an array as rows × row-length and name the total without counting every square.
I can split a row length into tens and ones and multiply each part.
I can add the partial products back into one total.
I can estimate an array product by the row length, not by the number of rows.

independent.prompt: The next panel row: 4 rows of 38 tiles. Split the 38 into 30 + 8 — what is the total?
independent.yes: Yes — 4 × 30 = 120 and 4 × 8 = 32; 120 + 32 = 152. The array's total is the two partial products added.
independent.notYet: Not yet — split the row length into tens and ones, multiply each part, then add the parts.

harder.prompt: The grove needs 5 rows of 47 tiles, but the row is delivered in two loads — 40, then 7. Show the partial products, and explain why splitting the delivery changes nothing.
harder.answer: 5 × 40 = 200 and 5 × 7 = 35; 200 + 35 = 235. The two loads are just the distributive property in two deliveries — 5 × 47 stays 235 no matter where the truck breaks the row.

options.task: An annotated array drawing of one panel row: the rows, the tens-ones split drawn across, the two partial products written inside their cells, and the total marked at the corner.
options.stem: ask which row to draw → plan the split → draw the array with the partials → test the total by adding the parts → share it at the dry channel

options.task: A tile-strip array model: paper strips for the rows, marked at the tens-ones split, so a classmate can read the two partial products off the model without seeing your work.
options.stem: ask what the model must show → plan the strips → build the marked array → test it on a classmate (they read the parts) → share it on the wall

options.task: A 60-second which-split-is-cleaner clip: ask the AI to propose two different splits of one row length, work both partial-product routes on camera, and say which split you would defend and why.
options.stem: ask what a clean split looks like → plan the clip → request two splits from the AI → test both routes on camera → share it on the wall

home: 4 × 213 on an area model: split the 213 into 200 + 10 + 3. What are the three partial areas, and the total?
Why does the area model show the same total as the array? What is a rectangle's area really made of?
Take 3 × 126. Split the 126 two different ways and show that both area models land on the same area.

claims: I can partition a number into place-value parts and draw the area model.
I can multiply each part by the one-digit factor to get the partial areas.
I can add the partial areas into one total area.
I can estimate the area first and tell whether the total makes sense.

independent.prompt: The roof panel count: 5 × 246. Split the 246 into 200 + 40 + 6 — what is the total area?
independent.yes: Yes — 1,000 + 200 + 30 = 1,230. Every panel of the roof is counted exactly once.
independent.notYet: Not yet — split the row length into place-value parts, find each partial area, then add them.

harder.prompt: The same roof: 5 × 246. Draw both splits — 200 + 40 + 6 and 200 + 46 — and show both models give 1,230. Why does the split not change the area?
harder.answer: Split one: 1,000 + 200 + 30 = 1,230. Split two: 1,000 + (5 × 46) = 1,000 + 230 = 1,230. The area is fixed by the two side lengths; only the partition lines inside the rectangle move.

options.task: A roof area-model design: draw the roof as a rectangle, partition it the way the class chose, label every partial area, and total the panels — sized so a classmate could price the roof from your drawing alone.
options.stem: ask how to split the roof → plan the partition → draw and label the model → test the total with a second split → share it at the gate

options.task: A partial-products chant for the roof: one verse per partial area, a chorus that adds them into the total — with a clap rhythm that carries the place-value parts.
options.stem: ask what the roof's parts are → plan the verses → write the chant → test it on a classmate (they total the parts) → share it at the dry channel

options.task: A partition map from a real roof: research one real long roof or fence length with the AI, verify it, then draw the area model for the panel count and map every partial area to a part of the real measurement.
options.stem: ask what real length to model → plan the map → research a real measurement with the AI (verify it) → test the model with a second split → share it on the wall

home: 3 × 2,146 — estimate first: round the 2,146 to a friendly number and multiply. Where must the exact product land?
Take 4 × 1,325. Split the 1,325 two different ways and show that both area models give the same total.
Why does rounding 2,146 to 2,100 lose something? Which region of the number went missing?

claims: I can estimate a four-place product by rounding the many-digit factor first.
I can create two valid decompositions of the same number.
I can compare two area models and prove they give the same total.
I can name the region of a number that a rounding choice throws away.

independent.prompt: The courtyard side: 6 × 1,182. Split the 1,182 into 1,100 + 82 — what is the total?
independent.yes: Yes — 6 × 1,100 = 6,600 and 6 × 82 = 492; 6,600 + 492 = 7,092. The 82 part still carries its own tens and ones — every region is multiplied in full.
independent.notYet: Not yet — multiply every region of the split, not just the big one, then add the partial areas.

harder.prompt: The same courtyard: 6 × 1,182. Split it again as 1,000 + 100 + 82 and show the third model also lands on 7,092 — then say which split you would defend to the council and why.
harder.answer: 6 × 1,000 = 6,000; 6 × 100 = 600; 6 × 82 = 492. 6,000 + 600 + 492 = 7,092. All three splits agree because the side lengths never moved — only the partition lines did, so the class defends whichever split it can explain fastest.

options.task: A fold-out courtyard model: build the rectangle from paper regions (1,100 + 82, or 1,000 + 100 + 82), fold it flat, then unfold it to prove the two partitions give one area.
options.stem: ask how to show two splits at once → plan the folds → build the regions → test both unfoldings → share it at the gate

options.task: A 60-second two-models-one-truth presentation: draw two valid decompositions live, compute both totals, and close with the sentence that proves they cannot disagree.
options.stem: ask which two splits to show → plan the argument → draw both models → test both totals → share it at the council table

options.task: An AI-audited decomposition report: ask the AI to propose a decomposition of a four-place product, check every partial area yourself, and write a one-page report recording where you agreed and what the AI missed.
options.stem: ask what a valid decomposition needs → plan the report → request a split from the AI (verify every partial area) → test the totals → share it on the wall

home: 5 × 18 without paper: 5 × 20 is 100 — what do you take away to land on 5 × 18?
6 × 49: why does going up to 6 × 50 and taking something off beat counting 49 six times?
Find a pair of compatible numbers that makes 8 × 25 easy in your head. What makes the pair compatible?

claims: I can round a factor up to a friendly number, multiply, and take the gap off.
I can regroup factors so the product lands on a friendly pair.
I can pick compatible numbers that make a product easy to hold.
I can check a mental product by reversing it — the other factor times the same partner.

independent.prompt: No paper at the gate: 7 × 98. Go up to a friendly hundred — what do you take away after 7 × 100?
independent.yes: Yes — 98 is two short of 100, so take away 2 × 7 = 14: 700 − 14 = 686. The gap times the other factor is all that leaves.
independent.notYet: Not yet — see how far the factor is from the friendly number, multiply that gap by the other factor, and subtract.

harder.prompt: The order now reads 9 × 198. Use the friendly hundred — show what you take away, and give the exact total with a check that uses a different move.
harder.answer: 9 × 200 = 1,800; 198 is two short, so take away 2 × 9 = 18: 1,800 − 18 = 1,782. Check with a different move: 198 × 10 = 1,980, and taking away one row of 198 gives 1,980 − 198 = 1,782 — the same total, two routes.

options.task: A 90-second no-paper strategy video: pick the day's gate order, solve it fully in your head on camera, and narrate the move — round up, take the gap off — as you make it. The written check comes after the clip.
options.stem: ask which order to solve → plan the narration → hold the product in your head → test it with the written check after the clip → share it on the wall

options.task: A friendly-number poster: one mental strategy per panel — round up, regroup, compatible pairs — each with the gate's own numbers, so the class can re-run the whole delivery from the poster alone.
options.stem: ask which strategies earned today → plan the panels → build the poster with the real orders → test each panel by re-solving → share it at the gate

options.task: An AI-challenged strategy map: draw the mental route for 9 × 198 — the arrows of the round-up and the take-off — then let the AI challenge the route; if it finds a shorter one, map that too and say which you would defend.
options.stem: ask how the route looks → plan the map → draw the arrows → test it against the AI's challenge → share it on the wall

home: 8 × 198 — three contractors propose: round to 200 and take away; split into 200 − 2; count 198 in eights. Which do you pick, and what do you take away?
Estimate 7 × 99 by rounding the 99 up to 100 — does the estimate land above or below the true product, and why?
Two strategies for one product: 5 × 44 as 5 × 40 + 5 × 4, or 5 × 50 − 5 × 6. Which is less work, and when would you switch?

claims: I can list at least two valid strategies for one product.
I can choose the strategy that is least work for this number.
I can say whether an estimate lands above or below the exact product.
I can defend the choice with a reason tied to the numbers, not to habit.

independent.prompt: The gate order: 6 × 299. The best move is a friendly hundred — what do you take away, and what is the product?
independent.yes: Yes — 299 is one short of 300, so take away 1 × 6 = 6: 1,800 − 6 = 1,794. One basic fact did the whole job.
independent.notYet: Not yet — find the friendly number, multiply it, then take away the gap times the other factor.

harder.prompt: Three contractors bid on 4 × 7,996: A rounds to 8,000 and takes away; B splits 8,000 − 4 and multiplies both parts; C multiplies in columns. Choose one, show the product, and say why the other two lose the contract.
harder.answer: A: 4 × 8,000 = 32,000; take away 4 × 4 = 16 → 31,984. B is the same move written in two parts — 4 × 8,000 − 4 × 4 = 31,984 — so A and B tie, and both beat C, whose column walk is slower here and still correct. The contract goes to the round-up: one basic fact, one take-away.

options.task: A 60-second contract defense: stand at the gate, name the order, pick the strategy, show the product, and give the one sentence that decides why the other two bids lost.
options.stem: ask which order to defend → plan the argument → choose the strategy → test the product a second way → share it at the gate

options.task: A three-lane strategy model: three paper lanes, one per contractor, each showing its route to the same product — the fastest lane marked, with the reason written on its label.
options.stem: ask what three routes to show → plan the lanes → build each route → test that all three land the same → share it on the wall

options.task: A strategy-choice map from real orders: ask the AI to propose three real gate orders at real magnitudes, verify each, and map the class's best strategy for each — with the take-away shown under the product.
options.stem: ask what a real order looks like → plan the map → request three orders from the AI (verify the magnitudes) → test each strategy choice → share it on the wall

home: The grove model needs 7 crates of 186 tiles. How many tiles are packed in total? How many more would reach 1,500?
Four cards each show two numbers. One card is not a model of the grove. How do you tell a model from a random pair?
Write the material-schedule line for one row of the grove: rows × tiles per row = total. Which number on the schedule would you double-check first?

claims: I can build a model of a situation with multiplication — rows × row-length.
I can tell a valid model from a pair of numbers with no model behind them.
I can solve a two-step situation: find the product, then compare it to the need.
I can read the unit's artifact — the grove's scale drawing and materials schedule — and defend one line of it.

independent.prompt: The grove model's second wall: 6 rows of 164 tiles are packed, and the wall needs 1,100 tiles. How many are still needed?
independent.yes: Yes — 6 × 164 = 984 packed; 1,100 − 984 = 116 still needed. Two steps, one model.
independent.notYet: Not yet — find the product first, then compare it to what the wall needs.

harder.prompt: The council asks: could the class have used 5 rows of 220 instead of 6 rows of 164 for the same 1,100-tile wall? Check both designs, and say which one the council should sign.
harder.answer: 6 × 164 = 984 — eleven-six short, so that design under-builds the wall. 5 × 220 = 1,100 exactly — zero tiles wasted beyond the wall. The council signs the 5 × 220 design: the product lands exactly on the need.

options.task: The grove's scale drawing and materials schedule: build the unit's own artifact — the grove drawn to scale, every row as rows × tiles, every total checked a second way, and the schedule signed by its maker. This is the product the class puts its name on.
options.stem: ask what the grove needs → plan the scale → build the drawing and the schedule → test every total a second way → present it to the council

options.task: The grove presentation: 90 seconds, no notes — walk the council through the model, the schedule, and the one line you re-checked last because it mattered most.
options.stem: ask what the council must see → plan the order → build the talk around the artifact → test it once alone → deliver it at the seal desk

options.task: A 90-second council Q&A clip: you defend the grove model on camera while the AI plays the council — ask it to challenge three lines of the schedule, answer each on camera yourself, and close with the sealed handoff to the two-digit workshop.
options.stem: ask what the council will challenge → plan the defence → record it → let the AI challenge (answer every question yourself) → test the answers → share it on the wall

wall.artifact: The grove model with its scale drawing, materials schedule, and the class's council defences
